ety.text: Latin ōsubor. English os Unadapted borrowing from Latin ōs (“mouth”).

senses.d: An opening or entrance to a passage, particularly one at either end of the cervix, internal (to the uterus) or external (to the vagina).

ety.text: Inherited from Middle French os, from Old French os, from Latin ossum, popular variant of os, ossis, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ésth₁ (“bone”), *h₂óst.

From Latin ossum, popular variant of os, ossis, from Proto-Italic *ōs, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *h₃ésth₁ (“bone”), *h₂óst. Compare Catalan, French, and Romanian os; Portuguese osso; Corsican, Sardinian, and Sicilian ossu; Spanish hueso.
